This research focuses on optimizing the transmission performance of underwater fiber communications.  A key challenge in these communications is the high occurrence of signal distortions and data losses due to water penetrating into the cable, especially around the cable's connections to the transmitter and receiver.  To address this issue, the study suggests utilizing a decision-feedback equalizer, which significantly improves the decoding accuracy of data.  However, this technique has a major limitation when it comes to handling errors, particularly those resulting from large water-filled sections of the cable, known as burst errors, which severely impede the transmission performance.  To resolve this issue, various transmission schemes were tested, including the implementation of error-preventing codes and transmitter diversity techniques, which either face technical difficulties in being field-deployed or fail to fully tackle the problem.  Notably, the study finds that combining a feedforward diversity technique with a recursive decision-feedback equalizer is the most effective method, yielding nearly ideal transmission performance very close to the theoretical maximum.  This approach was successfully tested in a real-world underwater fiber transmission trial over a distance of one kilometer, using a data rate of 10Gbit/s and demonstrating its superior performance over other methods.  The study finds that the best approach is particularly resistant to specific types of distortions and data losses, known as water-clad and air-clad distortions, especially in larger cable sections.  This research provides valuable insights that can be applied to the transmission of fiber communications in other harsh environments.  The study further reveals that the best technique is most efficient when the water-filled section of the cable is relatively short, specifically less than 50cm.  Additionally, the study is the first to set a new benchmark for the transmission performance of underwater fiber communications, achieving a 10Gbit/s data rate over a distance of 1km with a relatively short 40cm water-filled section, and sets a new standard for future research in this field.  The study's findings can be applied to the transmission of fiber communications in other harsh environments, and it is the first study to test the transmission performance of underwater fiber communications over a distance of 1km. Our approach is unique in its use of special equivariant layers that enable efficient processing of 3D object data. By applying these layers to both image data and 3D descriptions, our network effectively mediates between these domains. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in predicting 3D object positions and orientations from 2D descriptions, as well as in generating 2D bounding box coordinates and orientation from 3D descriptions. The SiD Detector, a calorimeter-based detector for the ILD program at the ILC, is designed with a silicon tailcatcher and a medium-sized central calorimeter. While effective, the SiD configuration has limitations in its electron reconstruction capabilities, particularly in situations with electron multiplicity greater than four. To enhance performance in these cases, the SiD Sensor concept modifies the detector design by replacing the tailcatcher and central calorimeter with a shower detector consisting of finely segmented silicon sensors. By doing so, the electron cluster size is significantly reduced, achieving the desired performance with a smaller number of readout channels. However, given the limited resources available for the ILD program, the SiD Sensor concept may not be feasible within the currently allocated resources. Consequently, a simplified version of the SiD Sensor concept is proposed, which retains the key performance benefits while accommodating the available resources. The proposed design maintains the needed performance for electron reconstruction in all applicable multiplicity scenarios. Furthermore, it provides improved performance in certain scenarios, notably for electrons interacting deeply within the detector, where the cluster size reduction is more significant than in the fully functional SiD Sensor design. The proposed design also facilitates more precise electron momentum resolution and improved rejection of jet background, thereby meeting the ILD requirements. The paper presents the detailed performance R\&D for the simplified SiD Sensor design. Meanwhile, the original SiD Detector configuration remains the preferred choice for the CeND detector in the CEPC, due to its superior performance in certain backgrounds, particularly finite magnetic field conditions. The paper also explores the SiD Sensor concept within the CeND detector design, suggesting it could serve as a suitable electron detector for the future CEPC facility, particularly when coupled with a birefringent electron identification system. The paper outlines the key performance figures for both the SiD Sensor design and the original SiD configuration, providing a comprehensive performance comparison of these two detector designs. The performance figures indicate both designs excel in jet background rejection, whereas the original SiD design excels in the case of finite magnetic field conditions. Conversely, the SiD Sensor design demonstrates superior performance in shower development beyond the calorimeter's central section. The paper also presents the electron momentum resolution performance for both designs, with the SiD Sensor design exhibiting better performance in certain scenarios but the original SiD design performing better in other scenarios. The paper outlines the key advantages and challenges of the SiD Sensor concept, highlighting the need for further development of the proposed shower detector design, specifically in the area of photon cluster separation

By reconfiguring AI model deployments to utilize isolated hardware modules, a researcher has found that it's possible to achieve a more secure form of inference, dubbed "confidential inference." The developed method holds promise for addressing the increasing cost of large language models, particularly in relation to cloud-based training and inference, as well as the emerging trend of hybrid training, which combines cloud computing with local device-based fine-tuning. The method's cost-effective, secure model deployment approach is not limited to large language models alone, but is an invention that is universally applicable across all machine learning models, making it an important innovation that will have a lasting impact in the machine learning community at large. We have conducted an in-depth examination of the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of the Gd/Cm solid solution series, specifically focusing on the $x=1$ end points, GdSn_3 and CmSn_3. Using a hybrid DFT approach within the GGA+U framework, we obtained detailed characteristics of these materials. Our computational findings reveal that both GdSn_3 and CmSn_3 possess the AuCu_3 structure type, featuring overlapping and separated electron clouds in their (110) planes. Notably, they exhibit similar electronic characteristics, with prominent contributions from the Sn s and p states and significant participation from the Gd (or Cm) d and f states. Our analysis also identifies the prevalence of the local moment rule in these materials. Analyzing the spin-polarized results, we observe a significant magnetic energy gain, with the orientation of the Gd (or Cm) moment dependent on the crystallographic direction. In contrast, our investigations of the solid solutions GdxCm_1-xSn_3, with x varying from 0 to 1, show that the structural and electronic properties exhibit little change, whereas the magnetic characteristics display a more complex dependence on the Gd/Cm ratio. Notably, the energy difference between parallel and antiparallel configurations decreases with increasing Cm content, implying a reduction in the magnetic stability when substituting Gd with Cm. This loss of magnetic energy could contribute to the reported absence of magnetism in CmSn_3 and might be a key factor in the experimental difficulties encountered when synthesizing this compound. Nonetheless, our calculations suggest that a metastable, antiparallel ground state could persist if energy barriers associated with spin fluctuations were sufficiently high. Nonetheless, further experimental and theoretical investigations are needed to fully understand the magnetic characteristics of CmSn_3. Moreover, our results indicate that both GdSn_3 and CmSn_3 are topological insulators, with a nontrivial Z_2 invariant, and that the time-reversal symmetry breaking, induced by the inclusion of an external magnetic field, leads to a topological transition in these materials. Objects within an image are not isolated from its underlying context. They are instead intricately intertwined with surrounding elements that can greatly influence their identification. Contextual information, when harnessed effectively, has the potential to drastically reduce the need for annotated training data, thereby enhancing the performance of object detection systems. Nevertheless, measuring the significance of contextual elements for a given system has remained a challenging task. Prior approaches attempt to gauge context but often do so without considering a crucial aspect - the inherent noise present in system predictions. In contrast, our proposed framework preemptively addresses this issue by first distilling the implicit contextual importance from model predictions, both internally and externally, before applying it to reduce the requisite annotated data for additional improvement. In order to investigate the complexities of object detection within contextual environments, we employ a robust set of diverse benchmark datasets featuring complex contexts alongside frequently analyzed object detection benchmark datasets. The results of our evaluations reveal that the incorporation of contextual elements is not uniform - some objects benefit substantially from their context, as evidenced by significant reductions in the required annotated data, while others, like those that are readily identified with minimal context, do not necessarily need the full extent of the available contextual information. Moreover, our framework's capabilities to evaluate the contextual aspects of objects in a systematic and quantitative manner have a practical application, as it allows us to gain a deeper understanding of aspects that current state-of-the-art object detection systems often struggle with. In order to achieve further breakthroughs in object detection, our analysis suggests that attention should be devoted to the most contextually demanding objects within a given dataset or environment. In order to validate our approach, we employed a method that integrates the contextual information with the object detection system, but further studies are needed to explore whether the implicit contextual importance can be incorporated in a manner that is more agnostic to the system in use. This article outlines the potential of a novel approach called Broadband Waveforming, which unifies the transfer of electric power and data within a wideband frequency range. Unlike traditional OFDM, the BWF framework isn't equivalent to single-input single-output (SISO)-OFDM or multiple-input single-output (MISO)-OFDM systems across the entire bandwidth. Instead, we demonstrate that certain non-binary BWF configurations can be made equivalent to specific SISO-OFDM or MISO-OFDM arrangements within certain sub-bands. Building upon these analyses, we identify the conditions under which a general non-binary BWF scheme can be substituted with a SISO-OFDM or MISO-OFDM system across the entire bandwidth. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for evaluating the superior performance of BWF arrangements relative to their OFDM counterparts. Furthermore, we introduce a simplified end-to-end modeling approach for data transfer in the presence of BWF, which can serve as a pioneering framework for designing optimal BWF protocols. This model is particularly useful for designing scenarios where data and power transfer gains exhibit different dependencies on data and power transfer rates. We also explore the application of BWF in multi-user scenarios and show that it is equivalent to multi-user MISO-OFDM in the frequency-selective fading environment. These results provide a valuable foundation for investigating the potential of BWF to achieve greater gains than both multiple antennas and multiple carriers. Reinforcement learning experiences difficulties in exploring optimal policies due to various obstacles, particularly high-magnitude random actions caused by noisy observations, which can result in substantial drops in performance. To overcome this challenge, a widely adopted strategy is to employ robust policy learning methods, which can derive benefits from expert guidance. Although collaborative reinforcement learning methods combining data from multiple sources can be beneficial, the traditional approach of sampling equal amounts of data from each source can be inefficient, especially when working with limited amounts of data. In such cases, the best course of action is to prioritize data collection from the source with the greatest value, i.e., the one with the highest standard deviation, as it offers the greatest potential for reducing search time. The resulting Variance Decrease based Experience Replay framework can efficiently minimize the search time by selectively leveraging sources with significant standard deviations in a more adaptive manner, leading to a more effective reduction in action space exploration. The proposed approach is theoretically supported and is capable of processing a wide range of data sources simultaneously, including both single-source and multi-source experience replay. The results of our experiments demonstrate notable improvements in learning efficient, optimal policies for both discrete and continuous action spaces in challenging reinforcement learning tasks. Our proposed model, MultiTalk, is a comprehensive dialogue system that's designed to tackle a variety of complex tasks. Unlike most current approaches that focus on straightforward turn-to-tune continuations, MultiTalk enables the generation of highly branching conversations, spanning many turns. To achieve this, it uses a unique strategy where the next sentence is predicted through an expansive tree-like structure, incorporating all preceding text. This involves making explicit connections between every sentence and every potential continuation, resulting in a massive cognitive burden. To mitigate this, we introduce a novel pruning mechanism called the Thin Tail, which systematically eliminates less relevant branches as the tree structure deepens. To create a dataset that can support highly branching conversations, we gathered annotations for continued sentences at every turn within multiple ongoing dialogue contexts. Our findings indicate that even basic variants of MultiTalk significantly outperform independent sentence generators, and that the Thin Tail approach yields substantial improvements in coherence and relevance. Moreover, our results show that modeling full tree structures is essential for accurately capturing the coherence of long sequences. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/THU-OGS/MultiTalk. Our model achieves the best performance in the Parthasarathi et al. evaluation on the Low-Cut dataset (0.182 vs. 0.194). A version of our paper has been accepted at the 2022 Conference of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 2022 International Conference on Computational Linguistics, and we have presented our work at the 2022 ACL Workshop on Recent Trends in Natural Language Processing for Machines. Our team has also released the Low-Cut dataset, a collection of continued dialogues available at https://github.com/THU-OGS/Low-Cut-Dataset. Our subsequent study, presented at the 2022 Conference of the Association for Computational Linguistics, reveals that current leading dialogue generation models struggle with high-cut data, and our proposed multi-talk model surpasses all competing methods on the Low-Cut-Dataset (0.182 vs. 0.194) and achieves comparable performance on the High-Cut-Dataset (0.266 vs. 0.257). Our analysis of the Low-Cut-Dataset's characteristics indicates that the dataset's limited size may be a major hindrance, and our subsequent study on the larger High-Cut-Dataset (released at the same time) yields similar findings. Notably, the Thin Tail strategy outperforms all competing methods on both the Low-Cut-Dataset and the High-Cut-Dataset.

This paper discusses current LHC experiments' capabilities and limitations in detecting tiny new physical phenomena, referring to signals beyond the Standard Model that remain elusive even at its highest energy levels. Historically, discovering new, very small effects took many years of searching, from the weak neutral current's 0.1% impact on three-body events in 1970s to the recent, precise measurement of rare muon decays' 0.4% effect. Although it may seem that our current sensitivity is quite low, the LHC can still find significant evidence of new physics if its effects surpass 13% in certain processes or 20% in others. With ongoing upgrades and the potential for a future 100-200 TeV collider, our sensitivity to new physics will greatly improve, and we will be sensitive to effects as small as 0.1% in the future. Until then, we can explore new approaches to old problems, and identify areas where the most significant potential breakthroughs lie. The paper is an attempt to provide a comprehensive summary of the current LHC's capabilities and what it can achieve with ongoing and future upgrades. It also covers in depth specific areas, such as high-energy photon phenomena, rare decays, jet and vector boson physics, and gravitational and other non-standard signatures. It collects in an appendix relevant information for theorists to keep in mind when constructing new physics models. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various artificial intelligence tasks, yet their capacity to adapt to continually changing datasets remains limited. Incremental learning algorithms address this challenge by enabling a neural network to gradually update its classification capabilities as new data becomes available. Although existing research has produced methods to tackle incremental learning from datasets with stable class imbalances, the issue of learning from datasets with emerging imbalanced classes hasn't been adequately explored. Furthermore, when new classes appear, existing approaches often rely on cold start techniques that fail to utilize the incoming data. This paper investigates the problem of imbalanced class incremental learning by exploring two key aspects: (1) how to adapt to incoming balanced data and (2) how to handle incoming unbalanced data. We propose a novel architecture named Balanced Incremental Learning Network, comprising two modules that address these challenges. We also conduct comprehensive experiments on the task of imbalanced class incremental learning and compare our proposed approach to five prominent incremental learning architectures. The results show that our proposed method outperforms the compared methods on the UCSD Pedestrian Detection, CIFAR-100, and Amazon Peculiar Product datasets. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates in the face of frequency disturbances in trapped ion systems. We first identify the critical requirement for symmetric initial laser conditioning across multiple motional modes. In the ideal scenario, this results in pure phase rotations between any pair of modes, achieving Molmer-Sorensen-like behavior on a mode-by-mode basis without the need for multi-mode processing. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability to generalize this technique for various gate angles through a variation of the initial laser conditions. Notably, we observed a high success rate of approximately 98% in the case of five-dimensional Hilbert spaces, despite introducing an additional phase shift between certain mode combinations. This phase shift, caused by frequency fluctuations, can be mitigated by adjusting the conditioning of the laser on specific modes. As a result, this new method facilitates the creation of robust, frequency-tolerant Molmer-Sorensen gates within trapped ion systems. Furthermore, this implementation offers a straightforward procedure for incorporating classical feed-forward control, enabling the creation of high-success-rate, frequency-resilient multi-qubit gates in these systems. Using advanced experimental techniques such as resonant and non-resonant inelastic x-ray scattering and x-ray pair distribution function analysis, we gained insight into the atomic arrangements within the peer group of barium titanate. Contrary to common interpretations, our data indicates that the absence of ferroelectricity in this temperature range is not a result of random peer arrangements, but rather can be attributed to a specific distribution of titanium atoms that prevents the spontaneous polarization seen at lower and higher temperatures. Our model shows that the peer arrangements within the a-b plane are disordered in a way that mimics the pattern found in the c-direction at the relevant temperature range. This model also explains the peer-induced ferroelectric freezing phenomenon and suggests a multi-PEL axis model could be applicable in this temperature range.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on materials whose electronic structure incorporates strong spin-orbit coupling and geometrically constrained electron flow, often referred to as relativistic electronic systems. Certain phenomena, such as superconductivity, topological insularity, and multi-band ferromagnetism, have been effectively harnessed in these materials. However, there is another crucial property that these materials exhibit - the absence of backscattering due to structural constraints, which forces Dirac electrons into non-trivial orbits. This property is generally accompanied by robust spin-orbit coupling, singular points in space, and the scattering of electrons due to structural distortions, all of which combine to create novel possibilities for the control of these materials' properties via structural adjustments. This article discusses recent theoretical predictions of a strongly linked Dirac metal phase in 5d element-doped SrnO m+1 (n=1, 2) perovskites that exhibit strong spin-orbit coupling and electron flow constraints within a honeycomb-lattice structure. This metallic state, characterized by hybridized Dirac bands and structural distortions that induce electron scattering, shows potential for optimizing its transport properties through structural adjustments. Investigations using scanning tunneling microscopy and theory also reveal the highly correlated electron distribution across the metal's surface and the structural metal-binding energy relationship. This relationship, which may enable the manipulation of these materials' electronic structure through structural changes, offers novel prospects for the design of materials with optimized transport properties. This article is an extension of the earlier published article in Phys. Rev. B 102, 115104 (2020). Additionally, experimental verification detailed in the enclosed supplementary file serves as an update to the theoretical forecast presented here. This experimental evidence includes the demonstration of low-energy linear-doped fermion dynamics via NMR relaxometry and the observation of structural metal-binding energy relationships via X-ray diffraction in the Sr1.92La0.08O2 perovskite compound that corresponds to the theoretical model presented here. This experimentally verified understanding of these materials' electronic structures may enable the design of materials with optimized transport properties. Additionally, the novel properties exhibited by these materials may also present novel opportunities for their application in high-performance devices. This understanding may further enable the exploration of novel physical phenomena in these materials through structural adjustments. This article provides an update to this understanding and the experimental verification details of the novel properties and the theoretical models presented here. This experimentally verified understanding of these materials' electronic structures may enable the design of materials with optimized transport properties.

frequencies. Another common technique to analyze periodic signals involves
computing the discrete Fourier transform of data and identifying the largest

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant challenges due to illumination variations, wearables, and image quality issues. Extending beyond traditional two-dimensional face analysis, 3D face analysis requires robust solutions to tackle difficulties caused by visible surface areas, occlusions, and pose-induced distortions. Existing methods often fall short in their ability to withstand these challenges, with many relying on constrained datasets and difficult manual landmark annotations for training. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel, fully automatic 3D face analysis framework called SADRNet, capable of executing two significant tasks: refining three-dimensional face alignments and reconstructing faces in depth. By producing both high-quality alignments and reconstructions, SADRNet can handle a wide range of input images and produce realistic face models. With these features, a dual facial regression network is triggered to generate intermediate outputs and a face reconstruction model guided by these annotations. The implementation of least squares method on this framework is regarded as the squared loss function, which is a well-established approach. When the design matrix and noise follow specific patterns, particularly those of i.i.d. randomness, extensive research on the asymptotic behavior of the least squares estimator has been conducted. However, the case where the time series data exhibits both structural breakdown and lingering stochastic components poses a more complex challenge. One promising approach to solving this issue involves using a knowledge-based method and a neural network method in conjunction. In this paper, a novel context-gloss enhancement framework is proposed, based on a combination of both methods. Firstly, a neural network is utilized to create both contextual and lexical learning-based representations for words with ambiguous meanings. Secondly, these representations are combined with knowledge-based glosses to improve the quality of context-sensitive representations. Thirdly, the combined representations are enhanced through a context-aware fusion mechanism to reduce the impact of unreliable knowledge sources. Finally, a score-based selection process is employed to select only the most effective knowledge sources for each word sense, thereby creating a more precise and context-sensitive embedding. The proposed framework demonstrates notable improvements over existing methods, with results showing a 1.3% increase in the overall baseline score for the SEMEVAL 2007 test data. The code for the proposed framework is also made publicly available online. Furthermore, an analysis of the effectiveness of different knowledge sources is also conducted and the framework's capacity for generating context-sensitive embeddings is examined through a set of supplementary experiments. The results indicate that the proposed framework outperforms other state-of-the-art methods using both general and specialized knowledge sources. Temporal activity detection in videos is a difficult task due to significant contextual information occurring both before and after the actual activity period. Contextual knowledge that exists outside the marked boundaries is often discarded under current common evaluation frameworks, namely the Temporal Activity Detection (TAD) challenges. The problem is compounded by the limited availability of reliable contextual information within the marked regions. The existing approaches often focus solely on extracting relevant information within the activity windows, neglecting the importance of external contextual clues. In contrast, we propose a novel framework, Dual Context Consolidation Network (DCAN), which differs from the conventional methods. DCAN selectively fuses contextual clues from the activity window, the pre-activity window, the post-activity window, and the entire video sequence. The network F is designed to prioritize the most relevant context across all time domains. The proposed framework has been thoroughly evaluated on the FMOD and TARTANTOO datasets for the TAD task, yielding superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods. The code for the proposed DCAN framework has been made publicly available at the following link: https://github.com/zhk1209/DCAN. The name DCAN has been derived from the context of temporal activity detection rather than the detection task itself, and thus the prefix 'DCAN' is used. The prefix can also be modified to other suitable letters as per the specific application requirements. The proposed DCAN framework has demonstrated exceptional performance on real-world temporal activity detection tasks, and it is now being explored for other detection tasks such as object detection and box refinement tasks. The current dominance of pre-trained models in numerous NLP tasks cannot be overstated, as they have consistently outperformed traditional feature-based approaches. These models have excelled in tasks that are typically categorized into three distinct phases: preliminary training, selection, and final assessment. In contrast, the ongoing learning phase selects from a constantly expanding range of models for multiple target tasks, a process that differs fundamentally from these other phases due to its high-dimensional, highly variable, and noisy environment. A critical aspect of ongoing learning is the consistent selection of a small number of models to explain complex data, a task that is fundamentally an example of feature extraction. While it is relatively easy to select models for individual tasks, the challenge intensifies when learning is ongoing, new data arrives, and there are substantial changes in data availability across multiple target tasks. To date, no study has examined the efficacy of pre-trained models in the ongoing learning phase. We introduce a novel benchmark called the "Ongoing Multi-Task Learning Benchmark" (OMTB), which comprises 16 diverse NLP tasks that reflect various spoken and written languages, different task types, and varying data sizes. When put through a series of trials simulating ongoing learning scenarios, our findings reveal that although pre-trained models excel in the initial trials, their performance declines over time, and they struggle to compete with models trained on static datasets. Our results also highlight the differences in learning dynamics across various language types, highlight the dangers of selecting models based on sole performance criteria, and demonstrate the effectiveness of a simple ensemble method in surpassing the performance of single models, even in the absence of target data. In OMTP, the challenge lies not in achieving high scores in isolated trials but rather in achieving sustained superior performance in ongoing learning scenarios. We conclude that the current generation of pre-trained models has significant room for improvement in the ongoing learning phase and that further research is needed to validate the claims often made about these models' universal applicability. We also emphasize the importance of conducting thorough evaluations under realistic ongoing learning conditions, as well as testing the robustness of models across a wide range of target tasks. In addition to introducing a new benchmark, we also contribute a comprehensive evaluation framework that is adaptable to any newly created or existing learning scenario. This framework is designed to be highly modular and highly transparent, and it is comprised of a variety of easy-to-execute commands using Python. We have made all of the models used in our studies publicly available, and we have outlined a variety of potential research directions that these methods have opened up.

We introduce an innovative technique called Learned Sparsification, which prunes unnecessary graph features effectively, reduces unnecessary connectivity between nodes, and accurately models crucial node relationships using a minimal subset of neighbors. By leveraging the Pregel computing framework, Learned Sparsification allows for flexible parameter management, enabling both significant reductions in model size and minimalism in node feature information. Our experiments demonstrate that Learned Sparsification achieves exceptional classification performance, outperforming state-of-the-art sparse GNN models, while also showcasing the method's capability to create more efficient, principled GNN architectures that prioritize node activation and reduce unnecessary connectivity. Our findings also indicate that Learned Sparsification can be used as a complementary technique to other GNN pruning methods, and our results highlight the method's potential to create more interpretable and effective GNN models. Soft tissue navigation is increasingly applied in minimally invasive surgeries that treat non-resectable tumors and allow surgeons to steer away from vital organs. To address this issue, a non-rigid volume-to-surface registration is necessary to accurately align images with changing tissue shapes. We present a novel approach to achieve this non-rigid registration, based on a biomechanical model that utilizes sparse data features to inform the process. The proposed method is also computationally efficient, with a registration speed of ~5fps on a GPU, making it suitable for real-time tumor tracking. Additionally, we explore the impact of using a simpler linear model on registration accuracy and find that our non-linear approach consistently yields superior results. In complex systems, identifying all types of interactions that particles may have with each other is a fundamental step in understanding their behavior. Typically, these interactions are either repulsive, attractive, or neutral, and sometimes, they can also be sensitive to temperature. However, in some cases, the conventional classification may not be sufficient as it overlooks the possibility of particles having multiple opposite behaviors, a phenomenon that has been demonstrated recently in a simple, two-component system of colloid-polymer mixtures. The project introduces an abstract representation of this phenomenon by introducing a binary code that represents the hidden properties of particles and their response to external forces. The code is composed of two temperature-based components, and the challenge is to decipher this code without direct access to the properties of the particles. The solution to this challenge is to observe and record the movements of particles at different temperatures and then utilize an automated machine learning algorithm to simulate the behavior of the system, thereby revealing the hidden code. The code is found to exist in a superposition of attractive and repulsive states, characteristic of particles that have not been exposed to an external field. The application of the field causes the code to switch to either attractive or repulsive, a phenomenon that is influenced by the initial state of the system. The project demonstrates the potential of using machine learning to study complex systems, providing a new perspective on the long-standing issue of the glass transition in colloid-polymer mixtures. The issue is shown to be relevant to the behavior of particles in a state of quantum superposition, a phenomenon that has not been extensively explored in the field of statistical physics. The project introduces the concept of a phase space that is occupied by the average properties of particles, rather than their individual states, and the potential for particles to switch from a state of order to a state of disorder, and suggests that machine learning can be used to study the average behavior of particles in a state of superposition, and to investigate the phenomenon of entanglement in a two-component system. The project also demonstrates the potential of using machine learning to study complex systems by highlighting the differences between a system that is studied directly, and a system that is represented abstractly. The project concludes by emphasizing the importance of studying complex systems through their abstract representations, and the potential of machine learning to make significant contributions to this field. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. Our analysis reveals that certain control methods can be less effective than others when super-spreader events occur frequently. The study provides a framework for examining integrated compartment and event dynamics in epidemiological models. By leveraging previously acquired knowledge, humans easily switch between solving different math problems. However, current artificial neural networks require extensive retraining when adapting to different problems, despite having an extensive amount of unsampled data available from across the internet. This project explores the idea of allowing neural networks to generalize across different tasks without being trained on the specific data, and the conditions necessary for this to be achievable, as evidenced by our successful application of this concept to the problem of image classification. A key insight of this project is that successful cross-task generalization relies on a combination of two factors: first, the ability of the network to extract fundamental features that are common to all tasks and remain stable even when the input data changes; second, the use of a memory system that allows the network to draw on its past experience when processing new input data. This memory system, specifically a retrieval module, allows the network to recover important details that were initially missed during its initial, unsupervised training, and allows it to switch to solving a different problem more easily. This is supported by a thorough analysis of different network architectures and the results of our experiments, which show that the best approaches to cross-task generalization involve a combination of a simple, unsophisticated network architecture that is easy to train and a sophisticated memory system. This allows the network to generalize across different tasks at a rate of 5-10%, which is on a par with its performance when trained on the specific data, and significantly outperforms a network that is only trained on the specific data used for evaluation. This project provides the first formalized framework for cross-task generalization that is applicable to any application that utilizes neural networks, and paves the way for the development of systems that can easily switch between solving different problems, such as language translation, style change, and missing data recovery. This is achieved by utilizing a memory system that allows the network to draw on its past experience when processing new input data, and the results of our experiments show that this approach results in significant improvements to the accuracy of the network, especially when the data used for training and testing is similar. This project also explores a new condition for successful cross-task generalization, known as the "low-switch cost", which requires that the network is easy to switch from solving one problem to a different problem, and this condition is met when the network is trained on data that is easy to switch between different classes. Our proposed framework, ATOMIC, represents a comprehensive knowledge base consisting of implicit common knowledge among machines. This atlas is designed to facilitate conditional inference by providing a context for statements. We distinguish our work from other knowledge graphs focused on machine-specific knowledge, such as WordNet and ConceptNet. These knowledge graphs detail the meanings of individual words, the relationships between them, and the inherent properties of entities and the world at large. In contrast, the ATOMIC framework encompasses the intricate web of interconnections that underlies all language and enables the derivation of implicit consequences from explicitly stated facts. We demonstrate the breadth and depth of ATOMIC by developing a set of condition-action rules that accurately predict outcomes in diverse tasks, such as predicting the effects of human actions and the inferences drawn from written text. These predictions, in turn, form the basis for evaluating the ATOMIC atlas itself. We hope this work will spark a broader discussion on the idea of a machine-specific knowledge base and the standards that such a database should adhere to. This discussion will be significant for any community that relies heavily on text-based inputs and relies on machines to interpret, reason about, and derive consequences from the information provided. This includes, but is not limited to, natural language processing, artificial intelligence, robotics, and decision-support systems. We also introduce a protocol for formally evaluating the ATOMIC atlas and any other machine-specific knowledge base. This evaluation assesses the breadth and depth of the knowledge base, the consistency of the rules embedded within it, and the ability of the rules to accurately predict outcomes in diverse scenarios. Furthermore, we outline a design for a rule-based reasoning system that should provide a reliable and efficient means of evaluating the consistency of the rules and the consequences of any action or statement. This system, in turn, should enable the detection of any potential inconsistencies or errors within the ATOMIC atlas. We believe that a robust and well-designed machine-specific knowledge base like ATOMIC has immense value in numerous applications and settings. This value stems from the ability of machines to derive consequences from the information provided and to detect any potential inconsistencies or errors. This, in turn, guarantees the reliability and accuracy of all decisions made with the assistance of these machines. The location and width of these conductance plateaus vary significantly in response to changes in the gate voltage. The observed behavior is characterized by abrupt changes at specific voltage thresholds, which some researchers attribute to a phenomenon known as coherent quantum phase-jumping. However, our study suggests an alternative explanation, suggesting that the mentioned coherent quantum phase-jumping is actually a manifestation of the Coulomb blockade. The proposed mechanism is as follows: the formation of quanta within the nanowire becomes impeded when the charging energy exceeds the Josephson coupling energy, which occurs when the length of the nanowire surpasses a certain critical threshold. This critical length is directly correlated with the average distance between quanta within the nanowire. The results of our study indicate that the charging energy, rather than the length of the nanowire, serves as the key factor in determining the blockage of quanta formation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the combination of a high critical length and a strong Josephson coupling energy allows the nanowire to support an average of two quanta within a specific voltage range, leading to a failure in the proposed theory that quanta formation is generally restricted to a single quanta state. The understanding gained from these findings is expected to contribute significantly to the further development and analysis of Josephson quantum circuits, in addition to systems that rely on the coherence of quanta within a nanowire. A blockage of quanta formation, as described in this study, may also present an alternative path for the decay of a quanta state, which could have a mitigating effect on the infamous problem of quanta collapse via annihilation. This note provides a detailed explanation of the method developed by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris for creating complete, transitive hypergraphs within a d-dimensional space. A key property of this method ensures that any two adjacent vertices in these hypergraphs are isomorphic. We further prove that using this method any two non-adjacent vertices can also be mapped to each other, thereby demonstrating it generates complete, transitive polyhedra. We also examine a related rule for constructing self-edges in these polyhedra. Finally, we outline an alternative approach based on a more general definition of their vertices. Additionally, we provide a theorem defining the parameters required for a d-dimensional complete, transitive polyhedron and offer a glossary of the terms used. Lastly, we explore potential applications of these structures in the field of computer graphics.

Unrepeatable Encryption was initially proposed by Haeusler to safeguard interactions against active adversaries in online gaming contexts.  However, our analysis reveals that the protocol fails to meet its fundamental purpose even when subjected to a weakly active and somewhat trustworthy compiler, and as such it cannot be utilized in settings where a strong attack is feasible.  A key flaw in the protocol is the issuance of non-reusable tokens that lack any association with the user's identity, making it incapable of preventing a variety of attacks.  Our research also presents an improved version of Unrepeatable Encryption, meeting the requirements for composability and retaining the protocol's core characteristics, and this new protocol is currently being employed by Google in their Chrome browser.  Although our new protocol offers security in the case of a strong attack, the standard repetition extension for Unrepeatable Encryption continues to be secure. Researchers require highly accurate measurements of neutron flux to perfect their experiments and achieve results as intended. Currently, the standard method for measuring neutron flux relies on conversion from activation of a surrounding material, such as polyethylene, but this method's limitations need to be re-examined. One major constraint is the difficulty in obtaining a comprehensive set of data for interaction cross-sections between neutrons and polyethylene, often due to a lack of suitable experimental facilities. The DARWIN experiment, a forthcoming dark matter research project, will involve significant neutron flux and therefore accurate assessment of neutron interaction cross-sections with various materials, including polyethylene. To contribute to this effort, a novel scintillator sensor designed for detection of gamma rays can also be used to collect crucial information on neutron-polyethylene interactions. By converting the scintillator's readings into spatial distributions of light, it can effectively distinguish between 1553 gamma rays produced by the decay of absorbed neutrons, even when polyethylene is 20 cm thick. This breakthrough method offers a more reliable measurement approach for neutron flux, one that is less prone to systematic errors. Furthermore, this research paves the way for the DARWIN experiment to accurately measure neutron flux using a much thinner polyethylene layer, or even substitute polyethylene with a different material of a known thickness. The resulting reduction in background noise and increased sensitivity to neutral particles will have significant implications for the experiment's sensitivity to axion interactions. The new method also allows for the detection of much thinner targets, which could significantly reduce the required thickness of polyethylene, or allow for the use of a different material with a known interaction cross-section, thus providing a reliable and accurate approach to measuring neutron flux. The technique demonstrated in this research can also be applied to detection of other particles, such as protons or alpha particles, and the novel 3D scintillator sensor design can be used in a variety of experiments and applications. The described technique can be implemented in the DARWIN detector to reduce systematic errors associated with the detection of neutrino activity caused by dark matter interactions. In our previous research, we discovered how sticking probabilities change with respect to relative velocity, temperature, and surface tension in a water environment among temperatures 200K to 300K, relevant to how grains interact as they move closer to the sun within a planetary system. This study is a continuation of that finding, delving deeper into how the water adhering characteristics are affected by the temperature of the protoplanetary disc. Since the temperature in such discs typically rises with the distance from the central star, specific ranges of temperature were examined in this study. For regions near the innermost part of the disc (up to 10 million kilometers from the star), water's sticking probability is limited by its frozen state. In warmer areas just beyond this boundary (up to 150K), water's viscosity increases the probability of sticking, but only when grains collide each other at low velocities. In regions from 150K to 230K, water's viscosity actually decreases the probability of sticking at higher velocities, but this negative effect disappears in areas above 230K, where water's viscosity increases the probability of sticking in all collision velocities. This research has implications for how grains grow into larger bodies within a protoplanetary disc, especially in areas closest to the star, and could have a lasting impact on the formation and composition of exoplanets discovered in such environments. Imitation learning is a well-known imitation-based approach that allows a single master robot to teach multiple student robots from its demonstrations. However, current imitation learning models are limited to linear task constraints and don't account for the fact that the student robots may have different physical properties than the master robot. As a result, the student robots may not only struggle with mimicking the demonstrated behavior but also need to adapt to these constraints and property differences. To address these challenges, we propose a new imitation learning framework, named EKMP, that allows the student robots to learn from the demonstrations of the master robot, despite non-linear rigid constraints and significant physical property differences. Furthermore, EKMP enables the learning of new actions that avoid barriers and prevent the student robots from colliding with their environment. To evaluate the performance of our proposed framework, we conducted extensive experiments on challenging household navigation tasks involving multiple moving objects and obstacles, and found that it produces high-quality policies that are not only mimicked by the student robots but also adapt to new environments. Additionally, our results demonstrate that EKMP outperforms existing imitation learning frameworks and produces more robust policies that can handle a wide range of physical property differences. Our proposed framework also successfully handled real-world demonstrations and applications, and we show that it can efficiently learn barrier-avoiding policies on datasets with a large number of samples. Lastly, our framework can be used in a variety of applications such as learning from expert human demonstrations, transferring knowledge to new robots, and learning from demonstrations in the presence of noise. Notably, this finding holds true even when the Rashba parameter is much smaller than the magnetic field strength. Investigating the model using the cluster dynamical mean-field theory, we identified the nontrivial topological characteristics of the Rashba Hubbard model through the calculation of the superfluid density and Berry phase. Moreover, we established that a spin-singlet trimer bound state, which forms in the superfluid phase, is responsible for the superfluidity when the Rashba parameter is significant, whereas a charge-imbalanced setup leads to the separation of two distinct trimer bound states with different spin polarizations, and we demonstrated that the Rashba parameter signs these trimer bound states, resulting in a nontrivial topology only when they have opposite signs. Conversely, when the Rashba parameter is negligible, the two trimer bound states become uncoupled and the system transitions to a normal superfluid state. The model's electronic analogs, such as graphene and transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers with gapped zero-energy points, may also exhibit spin-singlet topological superfluidity when subjected to Rashba interaction, and potentially also in systems with negative dielectric constants and halogen atom lattices. Utilizing this technique, we measured the angle distribution at different densities and discovered that the average angle deviates from 90 degrees, ultimately identifying a previously unobserved phase transition at high densities where the angle shrinks to 45 degrees. This finding is supported by multiple experimental probes, and our results demonstrate that the vortex lattice exhibits a more robust and stable "square-square" structure in a region between the triangular-to-square phase transition and the high-density vortex-liquid region. This newly discovered "square-square" phase is expected to function as a robust platform for manifesting novel phenomena arising from spatial vortex pairing. Moreover, the results suggest that the "square-square" structure may serve as an ideal medium for enhancing interlayer tunneling and facilitating interlayer synchronization in fractal phases. As role-playing games shift towards digital platforms, the need for more human-like AI guides has increased. In collaborative settings like Dungeons and Dragons, the relationship between players and guides is particularly significant due to its social and interactive nature. A key aspect of this interaction is the directive language used by guides to navigate players through the game world. Current approaches to game guidance often rely on pre-programmed paths and static goals, but these fail to capture the dynamic, goal-oriented mindset of human players and guides alike. In response, our proposed framework for an AI Dungeon Supervisor learns to understand the intentions and mindset of both its human partners, allowing it to effectively communicate and direct the game's progression through natural language. By incorporating a hierarchical attention mechanism into a neural network that processes both action suggestions and narrative input, the AI supervisor can accurately infer the underlying goals and priorities driving the game's progression, and thus provide more engaging and challenging experiences for players. When evaluated against a dataset of recorded D&D sessions, our results show that this framework achieves a notable improvement over baseline models, and with the addition of a form of bidirectional communication, even better aligns the game's progression with the intended goals, resulting in a more satisfying and coherent story. Moreover, the integration of a contextual action suggestion model allows the AI supervisor to effectively navigate complex, dynamic scenarios, and the incorporation of a narrative-aware goal inference component yields more plausible and coherent goals that reflect the game's narrative developments. Through a design that decouples the goal inference and action suggestion components, the AI supervisor can efficiently learn from experience, and the paper's results with a dataset of over 10,000 action suggestions demonstrate the effectiveness of this design in achieving more optimal game outcomes. Furthermore, the proposed framework holds the answer to fundamental questions regarding the learning of direction language in collaborative games, and the paper's findings with both simulated and actual D&D games provide a wealth of information on the critical elements that these games require. The integrated design of the AI supervisor framework, with its bidirectional communication, hierarchical attention model, and contextual action suggestion model, may also offer valuable insights for other complex, collaborative scenarios that involve the learning of human direction and guidance. Classifying instances with multiple associated labels, a single instance being tied to multiple categories, is known as multi-label classification. Unlike traditional single-label classification which only deals with individual labels, this task tackles all labels at once. Although sometimes it seems feasible to obtain all labels for a given instance at once, as shown in our later submissions, in certain scenarios, labels are only accessible one at a time. When only individual positive labels are available, techniques and resources used in multi-label learning may no longer apply, making existing data without explicit label connections useless. This paper investigates the effectiveness of a method that can leverage such data to generate a useful feature representation for a model, allowing the model to learn from a broader data set compared to a single label classification system. Experimental results on six datasets demonstrate that by using just individual positive labels, a model can still learn a useful representation that is more accurate than a single label classification system. Furthermore, combining the feature representation from all labels yields an even more accurate model, close to one that is trained on explicit multi-label instances. The proposed method can be seen as a way to extract implicit multi-label instances from individual positive labels, and is particularly valuable in scenarios where obtaining all labels at once is not feasible. The source of gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting large amounts of radio waves remains a mystery.  Hadronic emissions from these galaxies are often negligible due to low particle energies below $10^{20}$ GeV.  In contrast, leptonic emissions may not account for gamma-rays above $50$ GeVs, as it would result in an overestimation of neutrino flux.  We propose a new model for gamma-ray production in these galaxies, suggesting that magnetic fields in the jet's tip can range between $10^2$ to $10^7$ Gauss, and prevent the conversion of magnetic energy into particle energy.  As a result, a significant portion of the jet's magnetic energy is retained, and when the jet meets the surrounding disk, this energy is released in the form of gamma-rays.  By applying this model to seven galaxies, we were able to explain the observed gamma-ray spectra, and account for gamma-ray flux above $50$ GeVs, as well as magneto-hadronic neutrino flux, without any additional inputs.  This model also predicts the presence of magnetic fields within the jet, particularly at the point of interaction with the disk, which can be verified through future observations.  This model may have implications for the absence of gamma-ray variability in these galaxies, and could provide a minimum disk mass of $10^6 M_{\odot}$.  Furthermore, when considering the detection of magnetic fields within the jet, we must choose between recovering the inherent magnetic field within the analysis, or selecting a more plausible current magnetic field that could result in neutrino and gamma-ray production.  This model highlights the significance of magnetic fields in jet physics, and the need to reevaluate the current framework used to interpret gamma-ray and neutrino data, with a focus on a more comprehensive multicomponent model.  Ultimately, this model emphasizes the importance of a non-zero magnetic field within the analysis, and the need to reconcile theoretical predictions with observed data in these extraordinary phenomena. However, such approaches can be circumvented by directly classifying heart sounds from various conditions. Furthermore, a new feature extraction method is proposed, based on the heart sound's time and frequency characteristics, and is tested and validated using the new database. The proposed feature extraction method is compared to a widely used alternative, resulting in a proposed approach that significantly outperforms the comparison method. The findings suggest that heart sounds can be accurately classified regardless of physical characteristics and background noise, achieving an overall accuracy of 89.44%. The accuracy of visual association detectors suffers significantly from the impact of erroneous positives in training data. This performance hindrance is attributed to the widespread distribution of misleading clues among training images, which misleadingly indicate connections between unrelated objects. The primary challenge lies in incorporating diverse, high-quality negative training samples that can effectively filter out these misleading clues. The long-standing issue with negative sampling is the difficulty in differentiating positive and negative labels, particularly for difficult-to-separate objects. Present methods often rely on manual labeling, resulting in time-consuming and inefficient use of expert expertise. Furthermore, the current framework of visual association detection is examined with a view to implementing an automated negative sampling approach, incorporating a professional-agnostic strategy that prioritizes challenging samples for relabeling. This approach is designed to be robust, efficient, and adaptable to various detection tasks. The proposed framework is named VisAN, and it is hypothesized that this approach will result in the creation of accurate models without the need for relabeling. The effectiveness of VisAN is demonstrated through a comprehensive evaluation of the MS COCO benchmark, and it is shown that it outperforms the current state-of-the-art models by a margin of up to 9.5% without relabeling, and achieves comparable performance to that of models trained with relabeling. The source code of VisAN is made available at the website http://www.wangyizhang.com/projects/visan.html.. This approach is further found to significantly reduce the performance gap with state-of-the-art models by as much as 5.4% when trained with only 10% of the original dataset, thereby demonstrating its ability to extract valuable information from small datasets. Additionally, VisAN is found to result in models that are less prone to forgetting, as demonstrated by a memory-based evaluation on the CUB-200-2011 benchmark. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design takes it a step further by incorporating a built-in parallel search function and input data filtering, making it an exceptional tool for optimizing database query performance.

In recent years, big data analysis has experienced rapid growth, but processing large amounts of information remains a significant challenge. One of the most effective techniques for solving this problem involves using a content-addressable memory, a type of memory that allows for efficient retrieval of specific data entries based on input data, a function that can also promote data learning and update functionality.

However, a major limitation of content-addressable memories in traditional computer systems is the serial search function, which significantly hinders their performance when dealing with complex queries and large datasets. To overcome this shortcoming, we have developed a Content Addressable Parallel Processor that uses multiple search units to conduct simultaneous searches, a unique architecture that allows for efficient filtering of input data and a control unit that orchestrates overall system operations.

By utilizing multiple search units, this processor is capable of handling complex queries with ease, even when dealing with massive datasets. The built-in input data filter, on the other hand, provides exceptional performance when handling queries with a high degree of selectivity, a feature that is often the case with many real-world database queries.

We have successfully built a working prototype of this processor using a Xilinx Virtex-7 FPGA, and our experimental results demonstrate its superior performance when compared to a standard memory system. The performance gains achieved with this processor are particularly noticeable in scenarios involving complex queries and queries with high selectivity, achieving speed-ups of over 10 times and 5 times, respectively. Moreover, our energy consumption measurements indicate that this processor uses significantly less energy than a system based on a standard memory, a key advantage that makes it an even more attractive solution for energy-conscious database systems. The extensive network of dark spots and facades on the surface of the star V2110 Oph, inhabiting a 2.5-day orbit with a M-dwarf companion, undergoes a transformative cycle every 42 days. Facades, representing high latitude magnetic features, display a 42-day cycle similar to dark spots, prompting the question of how they relate to the star's rotational period. If the star's rotation is exactly synchronized with the facades, both its latitude and amplitude would need to drastically change, a scenario that is unlikely. Alternatively, this system may harbor a planetary body, whose gravitational impact causes the star's angular momentum to fluctuate. However, the currently observed data do not provide sufficient evidence for this theory, and a more plausible explanation could be a previously unseen angular momentum transfer mechanism. Future observations with high-cadence light curves will be crucial in furthering our understanding of this complex stellar system.

We introduce a novel, multi-task learning model that integrates attribute extraction from various descriptions regarding a specific object or concept. This model incorporates two main components: an image encoder that treats object identification as a feature extraction task and a text encoder that is trained using a contrastive learning approach. For text encoding, we employ a contrastive learning method that enables the model to learn object-specific attributes from natural language descriptions. We also introduce a technique for integrating the feature extracts from text and an object's actual image. Working with categorical data in high-dimensional spaces presents a significant challenge, as it often results in a sparse and irregular variable selection problem. Despite the potential for great benefit, fully utilizing this type of data is difficult due to the large number of possible combinations it can take. For example, if a dataset has 50 different categories, it can take over 3 billion unique combinations, making it necessary to condense this data into a more manageable binary or categorical form. This reduction process, however, can result in a loss of information and make it essential to develop statistical methods that can effectively handle such data. The Group Lasso is a popular such method but can result in an overly sparse model due to its use of a single $\ell_1$ penalty, making it necessary to modify the method to accommodate multiple groups of variables. This paper presents an optimized version of the Group Lasso, named Enhanced Group Lasso, that incorporates distinct penalties for each group to achieve a more efficient and sparse model. This new method demonstrates several advantages over the standard Group Lasso, including a more stable performance, a sparser coefficient estimate, and the ability to handle soft-thresholding. Furthermore, this paper provides an algorithm for solving the EG-Lasso problem, along with a theoretical justification for the choice of its parameters. The results of our experiments show that the Enhanced Group Lasso yields more stable and sparse estimates than the standard Group Lasso, and that the method is particularly effective in handling categorical features with a small number of large values. We also find that the technique can result in a more efficient variable selection, a more consistent performance, and a greater accuracy in our experiments with real and synthetic datasets. To effectively separate mixed speech from background noise using deep neural networks, this paper presents a dual-path RNN model called DPCRN. This network is composed of two main components: a front-end layer that incorporates dual-path convolutional layers to extract noise-resistant feature representations, and a back-end layer that utilizes a recurrent layer to model individual speech sources. Experimentation reveals that this dual-path approach yields superior performance to homogeneous RNNs and baseline methods, as measured by the average source signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and perceived speech quality. Evaluations are conducted using the WSJ0-2mix dataset and a 2-speech-mixture separation task. Results show DPCRN's efficacy in processing more complex mixtures and the implications of these findings are discussed in the context of future network design. Implementation details and additional evaluation results are also included. The proposed DPCRN achieves an average source SNR of 12.54 dB and a PESQ score of 3.13, outperforming the current state-of-the-art model, the Convolutional RNN (C-RNN), by 2.35 dB in SNR and 0.11 in PESQ. The model's ability to generalize is demonstrated by improving the PESQ score of the secondary speech source from 2.19 to 3.15 when the easier primary speech source is separated. The source code for the DPCRN model is available online. The model's performance is further analyzed with a confusion matrix and source confidence maps, indicating accurate estimation of speech source activity in 81.11% of cases. Many applications of learning robotics require observations from multiple agents, such as a human and a robot, working together. Traditionally, training these systems is based on having expert demonstrations from each agent. However, this approach is limited because it relies on the presence of multiple expert providers and the difficulty of conveying joint observations effectively. This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to learn from just individual expert demonstrations without needing communication of joint observations. The approach is unique in its use of peer agents that do not provide demonstrations but are involved in the training process. This is achieved by first modeling the relationship between the agents' observations and actions using transfer learning and then utilizing reinforcement learning to optimize the behavior of the agents based on their own observations and the outcomes of the peer agents' actions. This method allows for the efficient training of systems that combine human and machine-based observations and enables the learning of a variety of tasks such as navigation and game playing from a single expert demonstration. Moreover, the method cuts training costs by at least five times when compared to training individual experts. The code for the paper is available at https://github.com/PRPR-Group/co-obs-learning. We examined the Aurivillius Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO) system using nuclear forward scattering and found that high pressure causes a significant increase in magnetic order within a four-layered Bi$_2$Fe$_2$Ti$_2$O$_10$ (BFT) layer. Under ambient conditions, BFTO exhibits antiferromagnetic properties, yet applying extreme pressure leads to a metamagnetic transition and eventually AFM to FM switching. A crystallographic transformation from tetragonal to orthorhombic occurs at high pressure, corresponding to a 45-degree rotation of the BFT layer. This structural change enables Fe$^{3+}$ ions to occupy equivalent sites, facilitating a transition from spiral to collinear magnetic ordering. Our findings are also supported by magnetic interaction energy modeling. Notably, this metastable FM state can persist even after pressure is released, suggesting BFTO's potential as a heat-sensitive FM material. Additionally, we observe enhanced diffusion in BFTO under high pressure, a phenomenon that may be utilized in the future optimization of this material's performance.

The classical shortest path problem has numerous real-world applications, especially in air traffic management. Due to the complex nature of flight planning, an alternative method solves a series of discrete shortest path problems in higher dimensional spaces. Nevertheless, relying solely on exact algorithms to determine optimal discrete shortest paths is not feasible due to their high computational complexity. Consequently, this paper proposes a probabilistic framework to establish error bounds for approximate discrete shortest paths, leveraging the properties of continuous shortest paths in high-dimensional spaces. A key challenge in this task lies in handling temporal relations, which are often not explicitly described and therefore, typically inferred from partial or absent timing information. In our research, we propose a novel concept of temporal relation representation - characterized by low-rank and model-agnostic forms. This representation is based on the assumption that temporal relations can be compactly represented by a minimal set of key periods, which are common across all events linked by a particular temporal relation. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we developed a unique multi-head relation encoder named Low-rank Temporal Relation Model. Empirical results from extensive experiments conducted on diverse and publicly available temporal knowledge graphs showcase the superiority of our Low-rank Temporal Relation Model over existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we explore the applicability of our approach to various temporal relation learning tasks and provide insightful analysis of our method's performance under different configuration settings. Our implementation is made available through an open-source code repository. Our research sets a new benchmark for temporal knowledge graph completion models, and our findings contribute valuable insights to the study of temporal relation learning. Additionally, we introduce a novel evaluation framework that assesses the efficacy of temporal relation representations. This framework complements existing evaluation metrics and provides a more comprehensive understanding of temporal relation learning. Our study also reveals the importance of model diversity in temporal relation learning. This is reflected in our proposed low-rank temporal relation representation framework, which promotes variety in temporal relation learning. In contrast, a model-independent temporal relation representation approach, which treats the study of temporal relation learning as a shape-fitting problem, prioritizes model similarity over diversity. This approach results in a model-independent temporal relation model that, while mathematically equivalent to low-rank formulations, performs suboptimally in our experiments. This highlights the significance of design choices made when developing temporal relation learning algorithms. Our study sets a new standard for temporal knowledge graph completion and our results demonstrate the superiority of low-rank temporal relation representations over model-independent forms. This is exemplified by our low-rank temporal relation model, which outperforms all evaluation benchmarks and maintains a balance between model complexity and accuracy. This is achieved through our novel relation encoder, which is both versatile and highly effective. Our study provides a comprehensive exploration of temporal relation learning from multiple perspectives, and our results showcase the efficacy of low-rank temporal relation representations. Autonomous systems, particularly those with limited situational awareness like single UAS, are constrained in their actions and subject to restrictive policies to prevent accidents and unauthorized behavior. These limitations are imposed due to the reliance of the system on a single perception module to interpret its environment. Unlike human observers who can assess a scene independently of their location within it, current artificial perception techniques are position-specific and narrowly focused on detecting particular features within a limited range. As high-hazard applications like collaborative UAS operations in congested airspace demand a more sophisticated and general form of situational awareness, incorporating separate perception modules into the swarm is deemed necessary. Each member of the swarm would then have a more comprehensive understanding of the situation, enabling more flexible and safe authorization of actions. This concept is initially put into practice using a simple independent perception module that recognizes other aircraft within the swarm, developed within the context of the NASA Phase 2 UAS Integration National Consortium. The new approach is then tested with a focus on detecting instances of safe and unsafe behavior from visual cues. Results show significant improvement in accurate and timely detection when the independent perception module is utilized by multiple swarm members, as opposed to the system using a single perception module. The independent approach also exhibits greater robustness in its performance. The developed independent perception module is comprised of a deep neural network that can operate independently of the UAS's main control system and provides situational awareness through a simple API. This approach enables the assignment of more general and flexible tasks to the UAS, as well as the incorporation of a higher-level reasoning module that can issue safe and unauthorized action alerts based on the situation. The approach's potential is further illustrated by incorporating the independent perception module into a model for controllability, and testing the approach with a larger and more complex scenario from the NASA Phase 2 dataset. The study demonstrates the ability of the approach to manage complex scenarios with multiple instances of safe and unsafe behavior, and demonstrates the ability to issue action alerts for specific situations. The approach's potential to be scaled up and applied to other domains is also discussed. The study's findings are also analyzed from the perspective of the field of artificial general intelligence.
